extracted.intended_audience: humor researchers, scholars of comedy, and practitioners (comedians, writers) interested in theoretical accounts of what makes things funny
extracted.subtask_description: Use Veatch's affective-absurdity (N+V) framework to analyze or compose humor by checking for a simultaneous 'normal' interpretation and a personally felt violation, and by calibrating audience attachment to the violated principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: N — Normal
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceiver's view of the situation is simultaneously a normal interpretation: nothing is felt to be wrong from one perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘N’ means the situation can be interpreted as ordinary/safe from at least one perspective; this normal interpretation keeps the perceiver from being upset. If N dissolves (no normal reading), the situation becomes offensive, frightening, or distressing rather than funny. Use cues that sustain a plausible ordinary frame to preserve N.

rubrics_metrics.name: V — Violation
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceiver simultaneously holds that some moral or affective principle that they personally are committed to is being violated by something in the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The violated principle must be a subjective moral principle—an affectively held 'ought' tied to the perceiver's lived commitments (e.g., family, religion, sexual taboos, decency, fairness, dignity, politeness, expected logical patterns). V provides the tension/incongruity that can generate humor; specify what norm is being transgressed when analyzing a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity (N and V together)
rubrics_metrics.description: N and V must be held at the same time for affective absurdity (humor) to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If V dissolves (no sense of violation) only N remains and nothing is funny; if N dissolves (no normal reading) only V remains and the response is offense or distress. Successful humor requires the perceiver to maintain both readings simultaneously—both the safe/normal frame and awareness of a personal violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment-strength prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: A perceiver's reaction depends on how attached they are to the violated principle: no attachment → no notice; slight attachment → V holds with N and humor occurs; strong attachment → V dominates and the situation is offensive or painful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use attachment as a predictor of individual differences and audience variability (e.g., dark jokes appeal to those only slightly attached to the relevant taboo). Assess whether the target audience's average attachment is slight (benign violation zone) versus strong (risk of offense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of 'moral attachment' (what counts for V)
rubrics_metrics.description: The violated principle must be one to which the perceiver is personally affectively committed—a subjective moral principle rather than an abstract ethical rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a range from strong-value domains (family, religion, dignity) to small-scale conventions (politeness, conversational norms, logical expectations). The stronger the affective commitment, the less likely a violation produces humor rather than offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative exclusion criteria (what N+V excludes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations lacking either N or V (or where V has been fully defused) are not humorous under N+V: pure surprise without violation; pure offense without a normal reading; resolution-only experiences where the violation has been fully removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an utterance, rule out mere surprise or mere shock as sufficient for humor. If a so-called joke provokes only offense (no normal frame) or only surprise (no sense of violated personal principle), it fails the N+V conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cueing/engineering N (practical production tactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A teller can engineer or preserve N by signaling 'this is just a joke' or otherwise cueing the perceiver to keep one foot in the safe interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical techniques include explicit framing, tone, meta-comments, stage cues, or other signals that create/maintain the normal reading alongside the violation. Failure to cue N increases risk that the perceiver will collapse into V-only (offense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and cultural calibration (prediction for variance over time/audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same joke will produce different responses across audiences and across time depending on audience attachment to the violated principle; cultural shifts in attachment can make previously funny material cease to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or assessing humor, consider target audience demographics, subcultural norms, and historical changes in attachment. A previously acceptable violation can become strongly attached and thus no longer humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist for applying N+V
rubrics_metrics.description: Four practical analytic questions: What principle is being violated? Is there simultaneously a normal interpretation that keeps the perceiver from being upset? What is the perceiver's attachment to the principle (slight vs strong)? Could a small change in audience commitment flip humor into offense?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist when evaluating or testing material. For production, iterate on cues to increase N and gauge likely audience attachment to land the joke in the slight-attachment (benign violation) window.
